Microsoft Copilot Studio · Cost Estimation

Estimating Copilot Credit Usage for Copilot Studio Agents

How to estimate what an agent will consume while you build it, while it runs, and once it is in production, with separate guidance for standard agents and Microsoft Copilot harness agents. Compiled from public Microsoft documentation · November 2026

The one thing to remember: identify the harness before you do any arithmetic, because the two harnesses need different math. A standard agent is estimated by adding up priced events on each conversation turn, and building it is close to free. A Microsoft Copilot harness agent is estimated per task, at roughly 100 to 500+ credits a task, and the meter starts the first time a maker types a prompt, long before anything is published.

Start here: which harness is the agent on?

Everything built in Copilot Studio runs on a harness, the runtime between what you author and the model that reasons. The harness is chosen when the agent is created, it cannot be changed afterward (there is no migration between harnesses, only a rebuild), and it decides which billing model applies. This page covers the two harnesses most agents are built on.

Standard harnessMicrosoft Copilot harness
Also known asStandard agents, classic and generative orchestration agents, agent flowsFormerly the GitHub Copilot harness. Microsoft Learn and the admin center still use that label, so search for both names. It does not require GitHub Copilot.
Best forRule-based agents, structured conversations, predictable answersReasoning-heavy, multistep business processes across many tools and files
Unit you estimateEvents per conversation turn, from a published rate cardTasks, each sized against published planning bands, then calibrated from measured usage
Build and testTest chat, flow designer tests and prompt builder tests are not billedNatural-language authoring, preview, and evaluations are billed, at runtime rates
Microsoft 365 Copilot license offsetYes, for authenticated employee-facing use in Microsoft 365 channels, with exceptionsNone. All usage is billed regardless of the user's license
Cost varianceLow to moderate, unless a reasoning model orchestrates the agentHigh. The same task can cost two or three times more on a harder input

How to check: in the Power Platform admin center, open Manage → Copilot Studio and filter the Harness column. Values are GitHub Copilot, Standard, or Copilot Chat. At scale, the Power Platform inventory has a ready-made "count agents by harness" query.

Two harnesses are out of scope here. Copilot Chat harness agents (the harness behind Agent Builder) bill like standard agents and can use the same method. The Customer Conversation harness, used for contact-center style voice and chat agents, is usage-based with its own per-conversation bands by modality. Size it from the Microsoft Learn usage-based billing overview, not from the figures below.

Standard agents: how they bill

Standard agents bill per event, not per conversation, against a published rate card, and several events can bill on a single user turn.

EventCreditsBilled unitWhat triggers it
Classic answer1per responseA static, author-written topic response
Generative answer2per responseAn AI-generated response grounded in knowledge
Agent action5per actionEach tool or connector call, trigger, topic transition, deep-reasoning step, or Computer Use step
Content processing8per pageDocument and image processing tools
Tenant graph grounding10per messageMicrosoft 365 tenant grounding, charged on top of the answer
Agent flow actions13per 100 actionsActions inside an agent flow. Each trigger execution counts as one action, including failed polling-trigger checks that never start a run.
AI tools, basic / standard1 / 15per 10 responsesAbout 0.1 and 1.5 credits per 1,000 tokens
AI tools, premium (reasoning)10per 1,000 tokensReasoning models, billed on exact tokens
Voice: classic / generative / premium10 / 35 / 75per minuteVoice channel. Core agent activity is included in the per-minute rate.
Reasoning models change the scale of the estimate. When a reasoning model orchestrates a standard agent, every model call in the turn (plan, search, answer) bills its tokens at 10 credits per 1,000, on top of the feature rate. Instructions, tool and knowledge descriptions, conversation history, and retrieved results are all in each call. Tokens read from the prompt cache are free; tokens written to it are billed. In Microsoft's own example, one follow-up message in a support conversation bills 141 credits, and the same question as the first message of a new conversation bills 461 credits. A non-reasoning model answering it would bill 2 to 7. If a reasoning model is in play, estimate in tokens, not events.

What the Microsoft 365 Copilot license removes from the bill

For authenticated, employee-facing use in Microsoft 365 channels by a user with a Microsoft 365 Copilot license, classic answers, generative answers, graph grounding, agent actions, AI tools, and content processing are not charged, within fair-usage limits. Agent flows are only covered when started by the When an agent calls the flow trigger during that licensed user's session. Three things are never covered and belong in every estimate:

  • Computer Use, billed for all usage.
  • Autonomous runs, such as an event trigger or a flow starting the agent, even inside a fully licensed organization.
  • External channels and unlicensed users, including customer-facing websites.

Standard agents: estimating the build

Plan the standard-agent build as close to zero credits. Testing in the Copilot Studio test chat, test runs in the flow designer, testing a prompt in prompt builder, and training an AI Builder custom model are not billed, and manual authoring never is. What can bill during a build is anything that runs for real in a development environment:

  • Autonomous triggers left on in dev. A trigger subscribed to a busy mailbox or table bills every time it fires, published or not.
  • Agent flows with non-agent triggers, including polling triggers whose failed checks still count as actions.
  • A published dev agent shared for user acceptance testing in Teams or a website, which bills at runtime rates for any unlicensed or external tester.
  • Computer Use rehearsals run outside the test pane.
Standard build budget (credits) = UAT sessions x credits per session (only unlicensed or external testers) + autonomous test runs x credits per run + agent flow test runs outside the designer x (actions / 100) x 13 + 20% contingency

For most standard agents this lands in the hundreds or low thousands of credits. Give the development environment a small capped allocation anyway, so a misconfigured trigger cannot spend production capacity.

Standard agents: estimating operation

Estimate one representative session per intent, then multiply by volume. Doing it by hand, even once, makes the stacking visible.

1

List the intents and their share of traffic

Group expected conversations into five to ten intents, such as "order status" or "policy question", and give each a share of total sessions. Use real ticket, call, or search data if it exists. A handful of intents usually carries most of the volume.

2

Price one session per intent

Map the typical turns in a session and add every event that fires on each turn: the answer type, any tool calls, graph grounding, flow actions, and AI tool tokens. Generative orchestration usually adds an agent action per turn for topic or tool selection.

3

Remove the share that is license-covered

Apply the covered share only to interactive, authenticated, Microsoft 365 channel sessions by licensed users. Autonomous runs, Computer Use, and external channels stay fully billed.

4

Add the autonomous and flow work

Autonomous agents are estimated per run: triggers per month, times the actions and answers each run performs. Count every trigger firing, not only the ones that lead to useful work.

Credits per session (intent i) = sum over turns of: classic answer +1 generative answer +2 each agent action +5 tenant graph grounding +10 content processing +8 per page agent flow actions +13 per 100 actions AI tools tier rate x (tokens / 1,000) Monthly interactive credits = sessions per month x sum(share_i x credits per session_i) x (1 - covered share) Monthly autonomous credits = trigger firings per month x credits per run Monthly total = interactive + autonomous, then add 10-20% Pay-as-you-go cost = credits x $0.01

Worked examples from Microsoft's billing documentation

AgentCalculationResult
Website support agent, 900 customers a day(4 classic x 1 + 2 generative x 2) x 9007,200 / day
Graph-grounded sales agent, 100 unlicensed users (50 licensed users are not charged)(4 generative x 2 + 4 graph x 10) x 1004,800 / day
Autonomous order-processing agent4 actions x 520 / run
Support agent orchestrated by a reasoning model, one message14,100 billed tokens x 10 / 1,000, plus feature rates141+ / message

Note what the sales agent shows: graph grounding is 4,000 of the 4,800 credits. In most standard-agent estimates, one line item drives the total. Find it before you refine anything else.

Standard agents: forecasting production

A pre-launch estimate is a hypothesis. A production forecast replaces your assumptions with measured unit costs from a pilot.

  1. Start with the agent usage estimator. Microsoft's public agent usage estimator covers standard Copilot Studio agents and several Dynamics 365 agents, aggregates multiple agents, and exports a PDF. Run low, medium, and high volume scenarios rather than one number. Microsoft recommends a 10 to 20% buffer and states the output is informational, not a quote.
  2. Pilot with one team or region for two to four weeks. From the Power Platform admin center, take month-to-date billed credits for the agent, broken down by feature. From Copilot Studio analytics, take the session count. Divide to get measured credits per billed session. Export session transcripts too; they cover only about the last 28 days.
  3. Re-derive the covered share from real users. Pilot groups are often more heavily licensed than the full population. Recompute the share for the production audience.
  4. Project volume from a business driver, not enthusiasm. Tie sessions to tickets, calls, or employees served. Ramp adoption over two or three months rather than assuming full use on day one, and add seasonal peaks such as open enrollment or quarter end.
  5. Re-forecast quarterly and after any design change that touches the cost driver, such as turning on graph grounding, adding tools, or switching to a reasoning model.
Production forecast (month m) = measured credits per billed session x projected sessions (m) x adoption ramp (m) x seasonality (m) + autonomous runs (m) x measured credits per run x 1.10 to 1.20 buffer

Microsoft Copilot harness agents: how they bill

Harness agents use usage-based billing. There is no per-event rate card to add up. Credits are charged for the model tokens, the tools used (including knowledge and MCP servers), and the harness runtime itself. Microsoft describes the cost of each task as a function of four inputs:

Models

Which models the task uses and how much reasoning it does.

Context

How much data, files, mail, and history is retrieved to ground the work.

Tools

How many connector, knowledge, MCP, and agent calls the task makes.

Runtime

The orchestration that plans, retries, and keeps work moving across steps.

Microsoft publishes planning bands per task in the Copilot Credits Guide. They are estimates, not commitments.

Runtime bandShape of the workEst. credits per task
LightFew sources, light reasoning, one or fewer outputs. For example, check an email, verify a workbook, post a status summary.100 – 300
MediumMany sources across timeframes, structured reasoning, two or more outputs. For example, compile an end-of-day operations summary and post it.300 – 500
HeavyBroad aggregation and deep reasoning over long timeframes, many outputs. For example, a multiyear compliance review distributed as a full report.> 500
Three rules that make harness estimates different.
  • No license offset. Creation and runtime are billed whatever license the user holds, including Microsoft 365 Copilot.
  • Billing starts at build. Natural-language authoring, preview, and evaluations all consume credits, on agents that may never ship.
  • Do not borrow Copilot Cowork's bands. Cowork's band descriptions read the same but its medium and heavy figures are higher (300 to 700 and above 700). Check which product you are sizing.

Harness agents: estimating the build

The build is a real budget line on this harness, and on most projects evaluation is the largest part of it. Split it into three meters:

Build activityHow it billsHow to estimate it
Natural-language authoringPer creation session, banded by conversation turns: light 1–2 turns (1–20 credits), medium 3–5 (21–60), heavy 6+ (61+)Authoring sessions x band. Usually the smallest line.
Preview and testingEach preview task bills like a production taskPreview tasks per maker per day x makers x build days x credits per task
EvaluationsEach test case in each run bills like a production taskTest cases x evaluation runs x credits per task
Manual configuration in the Build and Monitor tabsNot billedZero
Harness build budget (credits) = authoring sessions x authoring band + preview tasks x credits per task + test cases x evaluation runs x credits per task + 20% contingency for rework Illustrative: 3 makers, 4 weeks, light-band agent (about 200 credits per task) authoring 10 medium sessions x 40 = 400 preview 150 tasks x 200 = 30,000 evaluation 30 cases x 6 runs x 200 = 36,000 contingency 20% = 13,280 total ≈ 79,700 credits ($797 pay-as-you-go)

The illustration is a modeling example, not a Microsoft benchmark. The lesson holds generally: preview and evaluation volume, not authoring, drives build cost, so size the evaluation set deliberately and run the full suite at milestones rather than after every edit.

Calibrate early with your own numbers. After the first few dozen preview tasks, open the agent's Monitor page in Copilot Studio, which shows total credits and, where available, which activities consumed them. Divide by tasks run to get a measured credits per task for this agent. Use that figure, not the band midpoint, for the rest of the build estimate and as the seed for the operating estimate.

Harness agents: estimating operation

Harness agents are estimated per task, and the volume driver is usually a business event (an invoice, a case, a request) rather than a user conversation.

  1. Define the task unit. One invoice matched, one report produced, one request triaged. If a task can fan out (one request spawning several sub-tasks or connected-agent calls), count the fan-out.
  2. Band each task type. Classify each type as light, medium, or heavy, then replace the band with the measured credits per task from preview and evaluation as soon as you have it.
  3. Use a high percentile, not the average. Task cost is skewed: hard inputs, retries, and long documents cost far more than the median. Budget against the 80th or 90th percentile of measured cost, or the top of the band before you have data.
  4. Keep evaluation in the operating budget. Every instruction, model, or tool change should be regression-tested, and every regression run is billed. Plan a recurring evaluation line.
  5. Add every interactive user. If people also chat with the agent, those tasks bill too, licensed or not.
Monthly harness credits = sum over task types: tasks per month x credits per task (p80-p90) + regression evaluation runs per month x test cases x credits per task + interactive tasks per month x credits per task then add 15-25% (wider than the standard-harness buffer, because variance is higher) Illustrative: accounts payable agent 4,000 invoices x 350 credits (measured p85, medium band) = 1,400,000 4 regression runs x 50 cases x 350 = 70,000 subtotal = 1,470,000 +20% buffer ≈ 1,764,000 credits ($17,640 a month pay-as-you-go)

Do this comparison before choosing the harness: a light harness task at 100 to 300 credits is 50 to 150 times a standard-harness generative answer at 2 credits. The capability difference is real. Make sure the business case carries the cost difference too, for example cost per invoice processed versus the cost of the manual work it replaces.

Harness agents: forecasting production

Because there is no rate card, a harness forecast is only as good as its measured unit costs. Build the forecast in stages:

  1. Pre-build: size each task type against the published bands, using the top of the band. Microsoft Learn's usage-based billing overview links a Copilot Credit Estimator for modeling demand before any consumption history exists; treat its output as directional.
  2. End of build: replace the bands with the measured distribution from preview and evaluation. If evaluation used realistic inputs, this is your best pre-launch unit cost.
  3. Pilot: run a time-boxed pilot in a test and validation environment with a fixed allocation. Track credits per task weekly from the Monitor page and the Power Platform admin center consumption report, and watch for drift as users bring harder inputs.
  4. Production: forecast as volume x measured p80 to p90 cost per task, plus recurring evaluation and ongoing maker work. Changes to scope or instructions tend to make tasks heavier over time, so re-baseline the unit cost after every release, not only quarterly.
Environment classificationWhat to forecastSuggested capacity posture
Exploration and prototypingMaker authoring and preview, per maker per monthSmall fixed allocation, tenant-pool draw off, organization-defined agent limit on every new agent
Test and validationEvaluation suites and pilot traffic for a defined periodAllocation sized to the evaluation plan, time-boxed, reviewed when testing ends
Funded productionTask volume, regression evaluation, and continued maker changesNamed cost owner, pay-as-you-go for continuity where the process is critical, agent limit set from the forecast

Remember that capacity is charged to the environment where the agent runs, not to makers or users, so forecast by environment as well as by agent.

Buffer10 to 20%15 to 25%

Turning the forecast into a budget and controls

  • Price it. Pay-as-you-go is $0.01 per credit, billed to Azure. Prepaid packs reset monthly with no rollover, and the one-year Copilot Credit Pre-Purchase Plan offers tiered discounts at volume. Both pay-as-you-go and the Pre-Purchase Plan draw down a Microsoft Azure Consumption Commitment, which often changes the funding conversation.
  • Share the pool knowingly. Prepaid Copilot Credits are shared with Microsoft 365 usage-based experiences such as Copilot Cowork and Work IQ, so a Copilot Studio forecast reduces what is left for them. Review both admin centers.
  • Set the agent limit from the forecast. In PPAC → Licensing → Copilot Studio → Manage agents, set a monthly limit near the forecast plus buffer, a notification threshold below it, and decide whether the agent should stop at the limit.
  • Contain the environment, not only the agent. Agent limits do not cap an environment. Allocate a defined amount and turn off Draw from the available capacity in my tenant where you need a hard boundary. Azure budgets on pay-as-you-go send alerts but do not stop usage.
  • Know the failure mode. On prepaid capacity, agents are blocked at 125% of capacity, including conversations already in progress, and agent flow runs are blocked separately. When a harness environment runs out of credits, makers also lose authoring, preview, and evaluation. A pay-as-you-go overage plan keeps agents running.

For the full set of controls and optimization levers, see the companion pages Evaluating & Optimizing Copilot Credit Consumption, Budget & Cost Alert Options for Copilot Credits, and What Changed in Copilot Studio Billing.

Estimation checklist

Standard agents
  • Harness confirmed as Standard (or Copilot Chat).
  • Top intents listed with a share of traffic.
  • One session priced per intent, every stacked event included.
  • Reasoning-model orchestration estimated in tokens.
  • Covered share applied only to licensed, authenticated, Microsoft 365 channel use.
  • Autonomous runs, Computer Use, and external channels fully billed.
  • Dev triggers and UAT sessions in the build budget.
  • Estimator run at low, medium, and high volume with a 10 to 20% buffer.
  • Pilot measured credits per session replace assumptions.
  • Quarterly re-forecast owner named.
Microsoft Copilot harness agents
  • Harness confirmed as Microsoft Copilot (GitHub Copilot in the admin center).
  • Build budget covers authoring, preview, and evaluation.
  • Evaluation set size and run cadence planned and priced.
  • Task unit defined, including fan-out.
  • Each task type banded, then replaced with measured cost from the Monitor page.
  • Budget set against the 80th to 90th percentile, with a 15 to 25% buffer.
  • Recurring regression evaluation included in operating cost.
  • No license offset assumed for any user.
  • Environments classified and allocations set per classification.
  • Unit cost re-baselined after every release.

Compiled from Microsoft Learn public documentation and the Microsoft Copilot Credits Guide, verified November 2026. The Microsoft Copilot harness is still labeled the GitHub Copilot harness in Microsoft Learn and the Power Platform admin center at the time of writing. Harness credit bands are rough planning estimates published by Microsoft, not commitments, and the build and operating examples on this page are illustrative modeling rather than Microsoft benchmarks. Rates, license-inclusion conditions, enforcement behavior, and pack terms change often, so confirm current figures against the Copilot Credit Guide, the Copilot Studio Licensing Guide, and your organization's agreement before making purchasing or architectural decisions. This page is guidance, not a contract.
